prose.summary: Developer advocates help technical users understand, adopt and challenge a product while carrying their feedback back to the company. They combine software credibility with teaching, content, events and product judgment. The role is not conventional marketing with code samples attached.
prose.day_to_day: The work includes building demos, writing technical content, speaking at events and answering difficult community questions. Advocates test APIs, notice documentation gaps and translate recurring user friction into product feedback. Current listings span developer tools, service management, data platforms, authentication and AI. Senior roles also own programs, mentor other advocates and coordinate closely with product and engineering.
prose.work_environment: The live sample includes remote and site-based roles, with substantial travel or event work implied by the role. Home location can be flexible while the calendar remains shaped by launches, conferences and community schedules. The work is public-facing even when it begins at a laptop.
prose.getting_in: Start with credible technical work, then prove you can teach it in public and improve a product from user evidence. Build a small application with the target API, write a clear guide and deliver a short talk or workshop. Engineering, solutions and product backgrounds transfer when communication is demonstrated rather than assumed.
prose.ladder: Early advocates own content, demos or a community segment. Responsibility grows toward program strategy, product feedback systems, major launches and leadership across developer relations. The path can branch into solutions architecture, product management, education or developer-relations management.
prose.suits: This work suits people who enjoy building enough to earn developer trust and explaining enough to make that trust useful. It requires comfort with public questions, travel and priorities that shift with product launches. It is a poor fit if you want uninterrupted coding or dislike being visible.
prose.misconceptions: Developer advocacy is not constant conference speaking. The evidence puts presentation and events beside APIs, product management, Python, TypeScript, content and community work.
prose.who_qualifies: Software engineers, solutions architects, technical educators and product-minded community leads bring adjacent foundations. They need both a credible technical artifact and public teaching evidence. Strength on only one side creates a fragile application.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: Listings cannot show whether product teams act on community feedback or merely collect it. Without an internal path to influence, advocacy becomes explanation without leverage.

steps.how: Create a working application that exposes real setup friction, edge cases and questions a developer will face.
Write a guide and deliver a concise talk or workshop that helps another developer reproduce the result.
Collect recurring questions, group the underlying problems and write a useful recommendation for product or documentation.
Answer technical questions directly, state uncertainty and know when an issue needs engineering rather than performance.

prose.tools: Presentation, event planning, product management, REST APIs, content marketing, social media, agent frameworks, community engagement, Python and TypeScript lead the current evidence. The strongest advocates use the product deeply enough to teach its sharp edges.

specializations.name: Technical content
specializations.why: It builds guides, demos and reference projects that developers can reproduce.

pros: The role combines technical work, teaching and product influence.
It offers broad contact with users and emerging implementation problems.
cons: Travel, launches and public work can fragment the calendar.
Some companies want promotion without giving advocates product influence.

faq.q: how do you become a developer advocate?
faq.a: Build technical credibility, then prove you can teach a working project and turn developer feedback into product insight. A public artifact and a reproducible demo make both sides visible.

faq.q: do developer advocates need to code?
faq.a: Usually. The current evidence includes APIs, Python and TypeScript, and technical users expect advocates to understand the product through real implementation.

faq.q: what is the difference between developer advocacy and developer marketing?
faq.a: Developer advocacy centers on technical education, community trust and product feedback, while developer marketing centers more on acquisition and campaign goals. Healthy teams coordinate them without pretending they are identical.
